title: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
content:
Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.
After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus:
Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core. ✨
Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.
A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.
The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.
Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.
If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.
Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.
Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable.
In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles. 
Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth.
Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.

report.summary: Google’s Suncatcher prototype satellite is online, running a Gemma 4 model on a single TPU for short inference bursts and writing a haiku about space.
report.background: Space-based data centers are moving from concept to prototype as AI compute demand strains terrestrial power and cooling. Google’s Suncatcher project aims to launch networks of close-flying satellites that perform inference in orbit, using solar power and eventually high-speed optical links. The prototype launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 with more than 100 other spacecraft. The effort is a classic Google moonshot: designed for 2030s economics, dependent on cheap, reusable launch—especially SpaceX’s Starship—and tied to Alphabet’s stake in SpaceX. Rivals such as Starcloud and Cowboy Space are testing simpler single-satellite inference, while SpaceX envisions larger orbital data centers with laser links.
key_points: The Suncatcher prototype is communicating with the ground after a roughly three-week commissioning process. It carries four Google TPUs but can power only one at a time because the satellite generates up to 1 kW, limiting each TPU run to about 20 minutes. That constraint complicates space-to-ground scheduling.

Ground engineers sent the first prompt to Gemma 4, Google DeepMind’s pre-loaded model, asking for a haiku about space. The satellite returned a short poem and also reported on orbital conditions. Google says the spacecraft is operating nominally as the test campaign begins.

The next tests will examine thermal stress and space radiation. Radiation can cause bit flips that corrupt data without triggering normal monitoring. Ground tests suggested inference workloads should be mostly resilient, while training would be more vulnerable—but Google now gets real orbital data rather than simulations.

If the TPUs perform well, Google plans to launch two more satellites in 2027 with higher power generation and inter-satellite optical links. Those links are central to Suncatcher’s vision of distributed orbital inference, setting it apart from rivals that expect to run workloads on individual satellites.

Suncatcher’s economics depend heavily on Starship becoming fully and rapidly reusable. Google researchers estimated SpaceX would need 1,800 Starship flights to match the learning-driven cost reductions of earlier vehicles. Alphabet’s stake in SpaceX links the two companies’ orbital data center ambitions, even as near-term AI pressures weigh on Google’s ad business.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Suncatcher is an early test of whether orbital inference can become a real compute tier—useful for remote sensing, maritime and aviation connectivity, and regions poorly served by terrestrial data centers. It also creates a proving ground for radiation-tolerant AI chips and distributed space networking. For developers, the near-term impact is indirect: expect research APIs, simulation tooling, and experiments in model deployment under extreme power and radiation limits rather than mainstream orbital cloud services. Regular users are unlikely to notice space inference soon, but it could eventually support low-latency AI in isolated areas. The bigger signal is strategic: Google is hedging against terrestrial energy constraints while its core ad business faces AI disruption.
report.tools: Watch Google’s Suncatcher project updates, Gemma open-weight models on Hugging Face, and JAX or TensorFlow for TPU-compatible inference. For orbital context, try Orekit or SGP4 libraries to model satellite passes, and SatNOGS or GNU Radio for ground-station monitoring. Radiation-tolerant computing literature and Google’s TPU reliability papers are also worth following if you want to understand bit flips and inference resilience in space.
